3.1.1 Skills Adequacy

While organizational structures provide the framework for cybersecurity, the availability of

adequately skilled personnel represents one of the most pressing operational challenges in ports

across all income groups. World Bank survey results, illustrated in Figure 11, underscore this reality.

When respondents were asked whether their organization possessed the necessary cybersecurity

skills to manage current risk and compliance requirements effectively, the findings revealed notable

patterns. Confidence in skill adequacy was lowest in low-income countries, with only a small

fraction of respondents expressing full confidence, compared to a higher proportion in upper-middle-

income countries. Crucially, even respondents from high-income countries reported only “partially”

possessing the necessary skills — suggesting a universal sense of being under-resourced relative to

the threat landscape and falling short of compliance requirements.

Policy

Effective cybersecurity governance needs to clarify who is accountable, which standards apply,

how compliance is enforced, and how resources are allocated to address risks across the entire

port ecosystem. However, there is currently no widely accepted, binding global framework for

port cybersecurity. While the International Maritime Organization (IMO) and the International

Ship and Port Facility (ISPS) Code provide foundations, their treatment of cybersecurity remains

limited. At the national level, roughly half of countries worldwide, specifically 104 out of 194,

as measured by the International Telecommunication Union’s Global Cybersecurity Index, have

cybersecurity legislation applicable to critical infrastructure. Fewer than half of port stakeholders

report full compliance with existing frameworks in high-income countries. This situation is even less

governance, controls, and measurable outcomes, enabling benchmarking, vendor integration,

and compliance across jurisdictions (ISO 2022; NIST 2024a). While not port-specific or globally-

binding, these internationally recognized models are widely applicable and increasingly relevant

in practice. For example, during the interview, Port Victoria (Seychelles) highlighted the value of

aligning with ISO standards, including to meet growing expectations from the IMO to strengthen

cybersecurity investment.

Taken together, the global governance landscape for cybersecurity in ports remains fragmented and

largely non-binding. While discussions to strengthen international regulation and coordination are

ongoing at the IMO, mandatory requirements for port cybersecurity have primarily emerged through

national governance frameworks, which are examined in the following section.

set objectives. It is maintained to track ownership and due dates for risk mitigation actions and to

monitor any changes to risk levels. Examples of risk mitigation actions, as well as further technical

Box 10 Return on Security Investment (ROSI) calculation overview

ROSI quantifies the economic value of a security control by estimating the avoided losses

relative to the control’s cost. It adapts the classic return-on-investment (ROI) approach to a

loss-prevention context, answering whether a given security expenditure is cost-effective.

Key inputs:

• Single Loss Expectancy (SLE): estimated monetary loss per incident (includes direct and

indirect impacts).

• Annual Rate of Occurrence (ARO): expected frequency of incidents per year.

• Annual Loss Expectancy (ALE): SLE × ARO. This is the baseline risk exposure.

• Control efficacy (mitigation rate): proportion by which the control reduces ALE.

• Total cost of control: acquisition, implementation, operations.

Core calculation:

• ROSI = [(ALE × mitigation rate) – cost of control] / cost of control
